newsitem.title: USA: FOMC voted 11-1 to keep U.S. rates steady Aug 20.
newsitem.headline: FOMC voted 11-1 to keep U.S. rates steady Aug 20.

text.p: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 11 to one at its August 20 meeting to keep short-term interest rates unchanged, and maintained its policy bias toward tightening, according to meeting minutes released on Friday.
Citing concerns about inflationary pressures, Minneapolis Fed president Gary Stern dissented in favor of an immediate tightening. Stern also dissented at the July gathering.
The FOMC has since met again on Tuesday of this week and elected to keep the federal funds rate unchanged at 5.25 percent, its level since January 31.

"Mr. Stern dissented because he believed that policy should become modestly more restrictive," the minutes said, adding Stern was concerned that "in the absence of a substantial and sustained improvement in productivity, the prevailing pattern of demand might engender an increase in inflationary pressures."
The minutes showed a "differing view" from most at the FOMC giving "more weight to the risks of rising inflation."
The "differing view" also found "a prompt policy action was needed to contain inflation and set the stage for further progress toward price stability."
While deciding to keep rates unchanged, U.S. policy makers reiterated their commitment to the preemptive monetary policy introduced in February 1994, the minutes showed:

"The prudent course at this point was to await further developments that would permit them to assess the possible need for some tightening with a higher degree of confidence... At the same time, it was emphasized the Committee remained committed to a policy that would resist a rise in inflation.
"Such a policy would entail moving in anticipation of greater price pressures and before they showed through to actual inflation."

The minutes further showed the FOMC adopted a tightening bias -- a "directive (that) would imply any tightening should be implemented promptly if developments were perceived as pointing to rising inflation."

One concern expressed by FOMC members regarding the possible implications of an immediate rate hike was that "policy tightening at this point might generate an excessive reaction in financial markets."

Concern about financial markets' eventual reaction to a tightening was raised "both because it was not generally expected and because it would represent a change in policy direction that might well lead to expectations of further policy tightening," the minutes said.
"Such a development could have serious adverse consequences for economic activity if the expansion was in fact already slowing to a more sustainable and less inflationary pace," the minutes added.
The minutes also showed the jury was still out at the FOMC regarding growth and inflation expectations.
The FOMC noted "increases in prices remained remarkably subdued for an extended period in relation to measures of resource utilization, notably the rate of unemployment."
The U.S. unemployment stood at 5.4 percent in July -- the latest rate reported at the time of the FOMC meeting.

Among the reasons cited at the meeting as possible factors accounting for the subdued inflation performance were "highly competitive markets... comparatively small increases in labor compensation... (that) appeared to reflect worker concerns about job security... as well as substantially reduced increases in benefit costs."

While FOMC members "cited a variety of indications that economic growth was slowing from a very rapid pace," they also acknowledged "the extent of the slowing remained uncertain and it was unclear at this juncture whether the expansion would slow sufficiently to contain pressures on the labor and other producer resources."

Also, the minutes said "the (Fed Board) staff forecast prepared for this meeting suggested the expansion would slow to a rate around, or perhaps a little above, the economy's estimated growth potential." The minutes did not spell out what the U.S. growth potential rate is.
